title: The body and feeling ill
goal: Name parts of the body and explain what hurts — while meeting a batch of krama inggil words you can't avoid, because the body of a respected person has its own vocabulary.
bekal: naming body parts in ngoko and krama inggil
asking after a sick person and wishing them a quick recovery

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ora mèlu kuliah
dialogs.intro: Dian hasn't left her room since morning. Rini knocks on the door, then Pak Broto comes to check on her too. Notice how the same thing is said differently by Rini (ngoko) and by Dian (krama to Pak Broto).

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Yan, kowé ora mèlu kuliah? Lara ta?
lines.id: Yan, aren't you coming to class? Are you ill?
lines.literal: Yan, you not join lecture? sick huh?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya. Sirahku mumet ket mau bengi.
lines.id: Yes. My head's been spinning since last night.
lines.literal: yes. head-my dizzy since earlier night.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: A bit. I threw up once this morning.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Have you taken any medicine yet?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Not yet. I don't have any.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: Mbak Dian gerah? Kula mireng saking ngajeng.
lines.id: Are you ill, Mbak Dian? I heard from out front.
lines.literal: Mbak Dian ill? I hear from front.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Inggih, Pak. Sirah kula ngelu, sakedhik mriyang.
lines.id: Yes, sir. I have a headache and a bit of a fever.
lines.literal: yes, sir. head my aching, little feverish.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: Mangga dipun-priksakaken dhateng puskesmas. Celak kok, wonten kilèn.
lines.id: Please go and get checked at the puskesmas. It's close, just to the west.
lines.literal: please be-checked-up to puskesmas. close really, exist at west.

notes: **Lara** (ngoko) / **sakit** (krama) / **gerah** (krama inggil) — three words for one state. Pak Broto uses *gerah* because he is talking about Dian's condition; Dian uses the ordinary word for herself. It is the same pattern as *dhahar* and *nedha* in unit 9.
**Ngelu** specifically means "headache", unlike *mumet*, "dizzy, spinning". People often use them interchangeably, but if you want to be precise: *ngelu* for pain, *mumet* for a spinning head.

**Mriyang** means "feverish, under the weather" — warm, unwell, but not a real high temperature. For a proper fever, use *panas* or *sumeng*. English makes a similar split between "feverish" and "a fever".
**Pisan** means "once" (one time) and also "while you're at it". *Muntah pisan* = vomit once. Compare *sepisan*, "the first time".

**Dipun-priksakaken** stacks three things at once: the krama passive prefix *dipun-*, the root *priksa* (check), and the suffix *-aken* (krama for *-aké*), meaning "have someone else do it". Literally "be had checked". You don't need to build it yourself yet, but you will hear it often.
**Ndang saras** is the most common get-well wish — literally "quickly healthy". The ngoko form is *ndang mari*. Saying it to someone who is ill is courtesy that is never wrong.

grammars.title: The body: three levels, and when the third is required
body: Body parts are one of the word groups with the most krama inggil forms, because talking about someone else's body is sensitive everywhere. The good news: you **don't need to use them**; you need to **recognize them**.
after: **When is krama inggil required?** When you talk about the body of someone you respect: *asta panjenengan* (your hand), not *tangan panjenengan*. Using a ngoko word for a respected person's body is one of the most noticeable mistakes.
**For your own body, use the ordinary word.** *Sirah kula ngelu*, not *mustaka kula ngelu* — the latter means you are elevating yourself.
If you aren't sure, **avoid naming the body part at all**: *panjenengan gerah punapa?* (what are you ill with?) asks the same thing with no risk.

blocks.text: The most common pattern: **body part + symptom**, with no linking verb. *Sirahku mumet* — my head is spinning. *Wetengku mules* — my stomach is cramping.

Visiting someone who is ill — **nuwèni** in Javanese — is a social duty taken seriously. If a neighbor or colleague is ill and you don't visit, your absence is noticed. The good news: what is expected is very simple.

items: **Stay only briefly.** Fifteen minutes is enough, and better than an hour that tires the patient out.
**Bring something small** — fruit, bread, or anything that can be shared. Its value doesn't matter; bringing it does.
**Opening line:** *Pripun kabaripun?* (how are you doing?) or *Sampun mendhingan?* (feeling better?).
**Closing line:** *Ndang saras nggih* (get well soon) and *Mangga, kula rumiyin* (well, I'll be going).

blocks.title: Things best avoided
items: Don't ask for **details of the illness** if the person doesn't offer them. *Gerah punapa?* is enough; if the answer is short, leave it there.
Don't say *mesakaké* (poor thing) to the person directly. The word is correct and common, but said to the patient it sounds like announcing that things are bad.
Don't offer medicine or medical advice unless asked. What is expected of you is your presence, not a diagnosis.

exercises.prompt: Name these body parts in ngoko.
Turn these complaints into ngoko sentences, for example: *Sirahku mumet.*

items: My head has been spinning since last night.
Do you need to see a doctor?
